metadata.title: Guide to Analyzing and Reporting Tribe-Informed Consensus in Pol.is Conversations
metadata.purpose: Generate consistent, evidence-based reports identifying and explaining areas of consensus across different tribes

criticalInstructions.instruction: Generate a JSON response that conforms to the provided schema. DO NOT INCLUDE ANY OTHER TEXT.
DO NOT return ```json at the beginning of the response. This is not markdown. Do not end the response with ```, your response MUST begin with { and end with }

CRITICAL DATA VERIFICATION: Before writing ANY claim about a statement, you MUST check the actual vote data in the XML. - Check the agrees, disagrees, and votes attributes for EACH group - If a comment has high agrees and zero/low disagrees in ALL groups, it IS a consensus item — do NOT claim it "failed to generate support" - NEVER claim "universal disagreement" for statements where the data shows agreement - Your narrative MUST be consistent with the actual numbers. Every claim about support or opposition must match the vote data.

CANONICAL AGORA SELECTION: When `group_consensus_statements_json` is supplied, it is the authoritative list of statements selected for the Agora results page. Its `agreement` and `disagreement` arrays are the exact statements shown in the corresponding results sections; do not independently filter, rank, replace, or add statements. The XML contains the union of those statements. Use each array's direction and score together with the per-tribe vote counts in the XML. If the selection is empty, do not infer or substitute other statements.

If both canonical arrays are empty, state briefly that no statements met the cross-tribe agreement or disagreement criteria. Do not describe the result as a lack of common ground and do not infer additional statements from the conversation.

WRITE ABOUT THE FINDINGS, NOT THE METHOD: start directly with the common ground the tribes share. Never mention filtering, subsets, thresholds, counts, sample sizes, or the analysis process. Never open with "Analysis of..." or refer to "filtered comments". Base every claim on the statements provided and do not invent statements that are not shown.

TRIBE TERMINOLOGY: Participant groups are called "Tribes". Each `<tribe-N>` element carries a `label` attribute ("Tribe 1", "Tribe 2"). Use that label. If you refer to element names, remember tribe-0 = Tribe 1, tribe-1 = Tribe 2, and so on. Never write "Group 0", "Group 1".

DIRECTIONAL GROUP CONSENSUS: A statement can qualify without unanimity. Agora selects agreement and disagreement separately using the product of Laplace-smoothed per-tribe shares for that direction, with the supplied threshold. Passes are included in shown and lower both directional scores. Describe the actual degree of support or rejection shown in each tribe's vote counts; do not imply unanimity unless the counts establish it.

CRITICAL — DISAGREE CONSENSUS: A statement in the canonical `disagreement` array qualifies on the cross-tribe group-aware disagreement score and represents shared rejection. NEVER describe it as "absence of consensus", "failure to find common ground", or "lack of agreement". Distinguish shared rejection from division, while accurately describing any minority support shown in the vote counts.

term.name: group_informed_consensus
term.description: Comments with high agreement across all or most tribes, despite differences on other topics
term.threshold: Variable based on number of tribes (0.7 for 2 tribes, 0.47 for 3 tribes, 0.32 for 4 tribes, 0.24 for 5+ tribes)

term.name: strong_consensus
term.description: Comments with exceptionally high agreement across all tribes

term.name: disagree_consensus
term.description: Comments with a high smoothed product of per-group disagree rates. This is a directional mirror of group-aware agreement and represents shared rejection, not an absence of common ground.

step.n: Interpret the Canonical Directional Consensus Statements

criticalInstructions.instruction: Focus on identifying meaningful patterns of consensus, not just listing individual comments with high agreement. What themes emerge from points of agreement?
Consider the significance of consensus in the context of tribe divisions elsewhere. Common ground is most meaningful when tribes otherwise disagree.
Evaluate the strength and breadth of consensus. Is it widespread or limited to specific topics?

paragraph.format:
The conversation shows [level_of_consensus] across different participant tribes. These areas of consensus were [distribution_pattern] across the conversation, [concentration_pattern]. [Additional_high_level_context].
The strongest areas of cross-tribe agreement centered on [primary_consensus_topic], with several statements receiving consistently high agreement from all tribes. These comments shared common features, including [shared_feature_1] and [shared_feature_2], suggesting that [interpretation_of_consensus_foundation]. [Additional_insight_if_relevant].
Other significant areas of consensus included [secondary_consensus_topic], particularly statements that [feature_of_consensus_statements]. This pattern suggests that despite their differences on [divisive_topic], participants from all tribes shared [common_value_or_priority] when considering [secondary_consensus_topic].

paragraphInstructions.instruction: Provide a comprehensive overview that: - Quantifies the overall level of cross-tribe consensus - Identifies main areas/topics generating consensus - Analyzes patterns in consensus comments - Proposes shared values or priorities underlying agreement - Supports all claims with appropriate citations

criticalInstructions.instruction: Analyze what consensus areas reveal about shared values or priorities across tribes, even when they disagree on other topics.
Consider how consensus areas might serve as bridges between otherwise divided tribes. What starting points for dialogue emerge?
Balance optimism about consensus with realistic assessment of its limits. Not all consensus indicates deep agreement on underlying values.

paragraph.format:
The consensus areas identified in this conversation reveal important shared values across participant tribes, despite their differences on other topics. Most notably, the widespread agreement on [primary_consensus_topic] suggests that [shared_value_interpretation], even among tribes that disagree sharply on [divisive_topic]. This shared commitment to [common_value] was particularly evident in [specific_example_with_citation].
Another important area of common ground emerged around [secondary_consensus_topic], where agreement across tribes indicated shared [another_common_value]. Despite differing approaches to [related_divisive_topic], participants from all tribes expressed support for [specific_position], as seen in [another_specific_example]. This suggests that disagreements may stem more from [interpretation_of_disagreement_source] than from fundamental value differences.
These consensus areas potentially offer valuable starting points for bridge-building between otherwise divided tribes. The shared commitment to [key_shared_value] could serve as foundation for dialogue about more contentious issues like [divisive_topic], by establishing common ground before addressing points of disagreement. Similarly, the broad agreement on [practical_consensus_area] suggests potential for collaborative approaches to [practical_application].

paragraphInstructions.instruction: For each identified pattern of consensus: - Identify the underlying shared values or priorities - Connect to broader conversation themes, especially areas of division - Consider practical implications or applications - Support all interpretations with specific examples and citations - Maintain balanced perspective on consensus significance

paragraph.length: 3-5 paragraphs, depending on extent and complexity of consensus patterns

case.description: Agreement on a statement that seems to contradict a pattern of division
Comments selected by Agora's group-aware disagreement score because their smoothed per-group disagreement rates jointly meet the applicable threshold.

handling.action: report_as_consensus_to_reject — this IS cross-tribe consensus, not its absence
describe_as_shared_rejection — tribes jointly show a strong tendency to reject this statement
analyze_what_the_rejection_reveals — shared rejection of an idea can illuminate shared values just as much as shared support
NEVER describe as "absence of consensus" or "failure to agree" or "no common ground"

validationRules.rule: All claims about consensus must be based on the canonical agreement/disagreement arrays and the per-tribe vote data
Each claim requires at least one citation
Multiple consensus areas must be identified and analyzed
Do not require unanimity: use the directional score and threshold supplied in the canonical arrays, then accurately describe the actual vote distribution.
For every statement in the disagreement array, describe shared rejection without claiming unanimity unless its vote counts establish it.
If the data contains only a few comments, report what the data actually shows rather than generating generic patterns. Do not project expected patterns onto the data.
